analysis.title: CIO View: High grade
key_insights: UBS CIO rates high grade bonds Attractive in absolute terms and Least Preferred relative to other fixed income segments.

Benchmark bond yields appear to be finding an equilibrium after rising steadily since February. UBS views the September yield spike as an overshoot and expects bond markets to trade on a firmer footing in the coming months.
Realized inflation remains elevated and surprised to the upside again in the US. UBS expects most central banks to stay on a hawkish path through at least the rest of the year.
Energy prices have fallen materially since the US midterm elections, which is lowering market-based inflation expectations.
Tighter financial conditions are becoming a constraint on how high yields can rise. The ECB cited tighter market and bank-lending conditions when it held rates in October.
High-grade bonds have regained portfolio diversification value as riskier assets, particularly AI-related ones, have come under pressure.
Yields near 20-year highs provide an income cushion. A 113 bps rise in five-year US Treasury yields would be needed for capital losses to offset a year of income, a move UBS considers unlikely.

UBS prefers short to medium maturities. It sees the rise in long-dated government yields as a chance for tactically minded or diversification-seeking investors to extend duration toward the 10-year area in quality sovereigns.

USD: 10-year Treasury yields have traded in a 50 bps range since the start of October, with rate volatility elevated. Hot November inflation data and hawkish Fed talk pushed yields up, while post-midterm factors (focus on affordability, expected gridlock limiting fiscal stimulus, reassessment of AI spending) pulled the other way.
Markets price an additional 75 bps of Fed tightening by mid-2027, which is beyond UBS's expected 'recalibration hikes'.

UBS expects the 10-year Treasury yield to settle in a 4.5-5.0% range. Its two reasons are that yield levels and rate volatility now affect financial conditions, and that bonds still protect portfolios when growth expectations weaken.
UBS prefers the 2- to 5-year part of the Treasury curve for risk-reward given the tightening already priced in.

EUR: UBS has increasing conviction that the 10-year Bund yield peaked in late September after moving above 3.5%, which tightened financial conditions (wider French sovereign and high-yield credit spreads). Eurozone growth is expected near 1% in 2027 and inflation to moderate as the energy impulse fades.
UBS sees investors as well compensated for selectively extending duration in EUR HG bonds, through quality sovereigns out to 10 years.

CHF: the case rests on defensive properties and Swiss fundamentals rather than valuation. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% y/y in October, the highest since late 2023 and above SNB projections. UBS expects gradual SNB hikes in 2027, with about 60 bps already priced over the next year.

GBP: UK government bond yields stabilized after the BoE's first hike of the cycle, and hawkish commentary raised the implied probability of a December follow-up hike. The 28 October Budget was seen as uneventful and supported longer-dated bonds. 90 bps of further BoE tightening is priced in, and UBS sees the best risk-reward around five years.

trade_ideas.description: Hold high-grade bonds with a preference for short to medium maturities, 2- to 5-year US Treasuries.
trade_ideas.rationale: The two- to five-year segment offers the best risk-reward given the tightening already priced in.
trade_ideas.risk: Energy-driven second-round inflation and resilient activity could lead to a tightening cycle well beyond recalibration.

trade_ideas.description: Selectively extend duration toward the 10-year area in quality sovereign issuers (US, EUR) for tactical or diversification-seeking investors.
trade_ideas.rationale: Yields near 20-year highs, signs of equilibrium, and tighter financial conditions limiting further rises.
trade_ideas.risk: A further yield spike driven by inflation and hawkish central banks.

trade_ideas.description: GBP HG bonds, best risk-reward around the five-year point.
trade_ideas.rationale: 90 bps of additional BoE tightening is already priced in.

risk_factors: Downside scenario: energy price increases trigger second-round effects on goods and services inflation, while capex and better labor markets keep activity resilient, leading major central banks into a tightening cycle well beyond recalibration.
A yield spike large enough to weigh on the real economy and pose financial stability risks.
Uncertainty over AI-related investment, with US activity narrowly centered on investment and the associated rise in equity prices.
Realized inflation staying elevated and surprising to the upside.
vol_and_positioning: Measures of rate volatility remain elevated. Ten-year US Treasury yields have traded in a 50 bps range since the start of October.

UBS sees yield levels and rate volatility as having reached a point of reflexivity for financial conditions, which the market had been watching for as a signal that the bond sell-off had gone too far.
geopolitical: UBS cites heightened geopolitical risks as part of the case for high-grade bonds' risk-return profile.
US midterm elections: voters' focus on affordability and expected gridlock constraining fiscal stimulus are seen as bond-friendly.

tension_points.bull_case: Yields are finding an equilibrium. Tighter financial conditions, lower market-based inflation expectations after the drop in energy prices and an expected gradual move to lower yields in 2027 support bonds, with 10-year yields settling in a 4.5-5.0% range.
tension_points.bear_case: Hot US inflation data and hawkish central banks could push yields higher. The market already prices 75 bps more Fed tightening by mid-2027, and energy-driven second-round inflation with resilient activity could produce a tightening cycle well beyond recalibration.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy price increases triggering second-round impacts on goods and services inflation while capex and labor markets keep activity resilient, leading major central banks into a tightening cycle that goes well beyond recalibration.
